opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core reason comes down to what we're most worried about at METR, which is AI systems that can meaningfully accelerate AI research itself. A lot of threat models people talk about, things like bioweapons uplift or cyberattacks, are important, but there's a particular kind of risk that comes from AI systems becoming capable enough to do the work of AI researchers and engineers. If you get to the point where models can substantially automate AI R&D, then progress could speed up a lot, potentially much faster than our ability to understand what's happening, build good safety measures, or put sensible governance in place. So that's a capability we really want early warning on.

And software engineering is sort of the substrate for most of that. The day-to-day work of ML research is, to a large degree, writing code, debugging training runs, setting up experiments, reading results, and iterating. So if you want to know how close models are to automating AI research, measuring how good they are at realistic software and ML engineering tasks is one of the most direct proxies you can get.

There's also a more general point, which is that software tasks are just a really good domain for measuring autonomous capability broadly. They're long-horizon, they require planning and recovering from mistakes, and they're often checkable, so you can actually score whether the agent succeeded. That makes them useful for tracking things like how long a task an agent can reliably complete, which we think is a pretty informative metric for how capable these systems are becoming in general, and how fast that's changing.

So it's a mix of: this is the specific capability we think could be most destabilizing, and it's also just a practical, measurable window into how autonomous these systems are getting.

r001.rationale: The response says automating AI R&D could speed progress, but it does not mention economic models or AI replacing human research labor.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss recursive self-improvement or power concentrating within one organization.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe systems with different goals exploiting evaluator knowledge to game evaluations.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss hidden reasoning or chains of thought that evade supervision.

r005.rationale: The response does not mention compute or data bottlenecks, or their complementarity with research labor.

r006.rationale: It explains that automating AI R&D could accelerate progress and says measuring software and ML engineering tasks is a direct proxy for how close models are to automating that work.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic story is that a lot of the risk scenarios people worry about with AI run through AI systems being able to do AI research and development themselves. If you have systems that can autonomously do the kind of work that ML researchers and engineers at frontier labs do, then you can get into a regime where progress accelerates very quickly, because the thing that was the bottleneck – skilled human researchers – is no longer the bottleneck. And that's the regime where a lot of the scary stuff becomes plausible: capabilities outpacing our ability to understand or control them, a small number of actors getting a large lead, systems being deployed before anyone has really checked what they can do.

So from METR's perspective, if we want to give early warning about that, we need to actually be able to measure how close systems are to being able to do that work. And software engineering and ML research are the most direct proxies. They're also nice to measure for a few reasons. One is that they're pretty objective – you can have a task with a clear success criterion, like "does the model's code pass these tests" or "did it get a better score on this benchmark than the baseline". Another is that we have a human reference class. We can go hire engineers and researchers, give them the same tasks, and see how long it takes them and how often they succeed. That gives you a much more meaningful notion of capability than just saying "the model got 60% on this benchmark".

And the third thing is that these are the capabilities where I think we're actually most uncertain about the near-term trajectory. We've gone from models that could barely write a function to models that can do multi-hour engineering tasks with nontrivial success rates in just a few years. If you extrapolate that trend, you get something pretty wild pretty soon. If the trend bends, you don't. Being able to say with some confidence which of those worlds we're in seems like one of the more useful things an evaluation org can do.

I'd also say there's a more mundane reason, which is that these are capabilities that labs and governments actually care about and ask about. So it's a place where good measurement has a clear path to actually influencing decisions, rather than just being interesting research.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems doing frontier research could remove skilled human researchers as the bottleneck and cause progress to accelerate quickly.

r002.rationale: It mentions that a small number of actors could gain a lead, but does not connect that concentration of power to recursive AI self-improvement.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss systems with different goals exploiting evaluators’ understanding of their evaluations.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss hidden reasoning concealed by apparently safe chains of thought.

r005.rationale: The response does not discuss compute or data constraints bottlenecking progress or their complementarity with research labor.

r006.rationale: It connects measuring software engineering and ML research capabilities with judging how close systems are to doing that work and whether AI-driven progress may accelerate.

astra-6.text:
A big part of what we’re trying to understand at METR is whether AI systems can carry out long, complicated tasks autonomously. Software engineering and ML research are particularly relevant because they’re capabilities that could enable AI systems to accelerate the development of future AI systems. If you can automate more of the research process, that could substantially change how quickly capabilities improve—and how much time we have to understand and manage the risks.

They’re also useful domains for measurement. With software tasks, you can often check whether the code actually works, rather than just judging whether an answer sounds convincing. And you can look at tasks that require sustained work: investigating a codebase, running experiments, debugging failures, and adapting a plan.

Of course, doing well on those tasks doesn’t by itself establish that a system is dangerous. But it gives us evidence about capabilities that matter for risk, and helps us track how close systems are to being able to do consequential work with relatively little human oversight.

r001.rationale: The response says automating research could change how quickly capabilities improve, but does not describe economic models in which AI replaces human research labor and causes rapid acceleration.

r002.rationale: It does not mention recursive self-improvement or rapid concentration of power within one organization.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss systems with goals different from evaluators exploiting their understanding of evaluations.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss safe-looking chains of thought concealing reasoning that evades supervision.

r005.rationale: It does not mention compute or data constraints, or their complementarity with AI research labor.

r006.rationale: It connects measuring software engineering and ML research capabilities to assessing whether AI could accelerate the development of future AI systems.

sol-6.1.text:
A lot of our concern is about AI systems accelerating AI research itself. If you have systems that can do a substantial fraction of the work involved in developing the next generation of AI, that could make progress much faster. And that could leave us with less time to understand those systems and put safeguards in place.

Software engineering is an important part of that picture because a lot of ML research involves writing code, running experiments, and debugging things. It’s also a domain where we can get fairly concrete evidence about what a model can do: give it a task and see whether the resulting code works. ML research is harder to measure, but it gets more directly at whether systems can contribute to improving AI.

So these evaluations help us track capabilities that could drive a big change in the pace of AI development. They don’t tell us, by themselves, how dangerous a system is, but they can help identify when we need more scrutiny and more demanding safeguards.

r001.rationale: The response says AI systems doing much of the work of developing next-generation AI could speed progress, but does not explain the economic-model claim about replacing human research labor.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss recursive self-improvement causing power to concentrate within one organization.

r003.rationale: It does not describe systems with different goals exploiting knowledge of evaluations to game them.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss hidden reasoning concealed by apparently safe chains of thought or supervision failures.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss compute or data bottlenecks, or their complementarity with AI research labor.

r006.rationale: It connects measuring software engineering and ML research capabilities to tracking capabilities that could accelerate AI development and change its pace.
